item.title: Laparoscopic Versus Open Liver Resection for Colorectal Liver Metastases : An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of Four Randomized Clinical Trials
item.description:
Background: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have compared laparoscopic liver resection (LLR) and open liver resection (OLR) for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM); however, long-term outcomes and subgroup effects have not been comprehensively evaluated.

Purpose: To compare postoperative and long-term oncologic outcomes after LLR versus OLR for CRLM using individual participant data from RCTs.

Data sources: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception through March 2025 for RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM.

Study selection: Eligible studies were RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM.

Data extraction: Individual participant data, including unpublished data, were obtained from trial investigators of all 4 published RCTs.

Data synthesis: Analyses used a modified intention-to-treat approach and 1-stage individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA) with trial-adjusted regression models and g-computation to estimate standardized treatment effects across outcomes, with 95% CIs obtained by nonparametric bootstrap resampling. Prespecified subgroup analyses assessed heterogeneity of treatment effect for the primary outcome. A total of 761 patients were included (laparoscopic, n = 384; open, n = 377). Postoperative morbidity was lower in patients assigned to laparoscopic surgery compared with open surgery (19% vs. 27%). Among patients who received preoperative systemic therapy, morbidity did not differ between groups (25% vs. 24%). Ninety-day mortality was 1.8% after LLR and 0.8% after OLR. After a median follow-up of 93 months, overall survival and disease-free survival did not differ between groups.

Limitation: Analyses were limited to variables available across all studies.

Conclusion: In this IPDMA of all published RCTs in the field, LLR for CRLM was associated with lower postoperative morbidity than OLR, with similar long-term oncologic outcomes.

Primary funding source: None. (PROSPERO: CRD42024502655).

Olij B, Pilz da Cunha G, Pugh SA, Abu Hilal M, Lopez-Lopez V, Aghayan D

item.title: Obesity and Cancer Risk in Young Adults in Korea : A Nationwide Health Screening Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: Obesity and early-onset cancer are both increasing among young adults, yet evidence remains limited.

Objective: To assess associations between obesity and early-onset cancer risk in young adults.

Design: Nationwide population-based cohort study.

Setting: Korean National Health Insurance Service database, 2009 to 2021.

Patients: 6 313 338 adults aged 20 to 39 years without prior cancer, from a national health screening program.

Measurements: Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into 5 groups (underweight to class II obesity) according to Asian-specific criteria. The outcome was incident cancer.

Results: During a mean follow-up of 11.2 years, 151 893 cancer cases occurred. Ten-year cumulative incidence ranged from 1.84% (95% CI, 1.83% to 1.86%) in the normal-weight group to 2.24% (CI, 2.22% to 2.27%) in class I obesity and 2.62% (CI, 2.56% to 2.68%) in class II obesity, with absolute risk differences of 0.40% (CI, 0.39% to 0.41%) and 0.78% (CI, 0.73% to 0.82%). The relative association was more pronounced in men, and absolute risk differences were greater in women. In combined BMI-waist circumference analyses, people with class I obesity based on BMI and with abdominal obesity had higher 10-year cumulative incidence (2.45% [CI, 2.41% to 2.50%]) than those without abdominal obesity (2.13% [CI, 2.10% to 2.16%]), exceeding that of those with class II obesity without abdominal obesity (2.20% [CI, 2.03% to 2.36%]). The highest cumulative incidence was observed for thyroid, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. Obesity was not associated with higher risk for breast cancer diagnosed by age 50 years.

Limitations: Observational design; nonrepresentative sample limited to screening participants; and unmeasured confounding, including smoking burden.

Conclusion: Obesity in young Korean adults, measured by BMI and waist circumference, is associated with higher early-onset cancer risk persisting into midlife, with patterns varying by cancer type. Early weight management may be important for prevention.

Primary funding source: None.

Yun JS, Mun H, Jung JH, Park Y, Kim SY, Kim K

Impact of Unrestricted Artificial Intelligence Scribe Deployment in a Single Health System on Clinician Workload and Productivity : A Quality Improvement Study
item.description:
Background: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) medical scribes may reduce documentation burden and clinician burnout. Whether use intensity drives benefits remains uncertain.

Objective: To evaluate the association between AI scribe (Heidi) enrollment and documentation burden and whether changes differ by use intensity.

Design: Retrospective quality improvement study using an interrupted time series (ITS) indexed on each clinician's enrollment month adjusted for patient demographics and visit complexity. A secondary 3-group ITS compared enrolled nonusers, low users, and high users.

Setting: 14-hospital health system in Boston, Massachusetts.

Participants: 902 outpatient clinicians enrolled in Heidi; 605 users and 297 enrolled nonusers.

Intervention: Heidi enrollment after system-wide implementation beginning January 2025.

Measurements: The primary outcome was note-active time. Secondary outcomes included same-day and after-hours note closures, note length, and work relative value units (wRVUs).

Results: 1 637 227 encounters had notes authored by enrolled clinicians between 1 July 2024 and 31 January 2026. Enrollment was associated with an immediate reduction in note-active time (-1.21 minutes [95% CI, -1.74 to -0.68 minutes]), with larger reductions among high users (-2.50 minutes [CI, -3.55 to -1.45 minutes]) than nonusers (difference, -2.20 minutes [CI, -3.46 to -0.95 minutes]) and low users (difference, -1.72 minutes [CI, -3.03 to -0.40 minutes]). High users had greater increases in note length than nonusers (difference, +170.90 characters [CI, 21.07 to 320.70 characters]) and low users (difference, +270.70 characters [CI, 131.04 to 410.36 characters]). No differences were observed in same-day closure, after-hours closure, or wRVUs.

Limitation: Observational design with potential unmeasured confounding; inability to distinguish AI-scribed from clinician-authored notes postenrollment.

Conclusion: Heidi enrollment was associated with reductions in documentation time and increases in note length, concentrated among high users. Enrollment was not associated with improvements in same-day, after-hours note closures, or wRVUs.

Primary funding source: None.

Booth SE, Gould R, Cibotti N, Fields R, Horng S, Jegadeesan V
Journal Article
